Hitopadeśa
(‘salutary instructions’)
------------------------------------------
Didactic compositions are a special feature of Sanskrit literature. Two of the more well-known works of such a type are the Pañcatantra of Viṣṇuśarma and the Hitopadeśa of नारायण, a court pundit of the king Dhavalacandra of Bengal.
The Hitopadeśa is a collection of fables and tales in prose and poetry. It has borrowed the material partly from the Pañcatantra and partly from the Kāmandakīya Nītiśāstra. It has four chapters:
Mitralābhaḥ (‘The winning of friends);
Suhṛdbhedaḥ (‘The breaking up of friendship’);
Vigrahaḥ (‘War’) and
Sandhiḥ (‘peace’).
King सुदर्शन had been very much worried by the lack of एदुचतिओन् and culture, and consequent indecent behaviour of his sons. नारायण promised to educate them in six months and, to the surprise of all, achieved it. The result was this wonderful work Hitopadeśa.
The Hitopadeśa contains a number of new tales and fables, including edifying stories, tales of intrigue and even fairy tales, but always aimed at teaching some great value, useful to life. It contains a good number of maxims and proverb-like statements.
The work has been very popular over the centuries and retains that position even now. It has been translated into thirteen foreign languages, let alone the several ones of India.
See also PAÑCATANTRA.

hita
(‘[that which is conducive to] well-being’)
------------------------------------------
Though this word in a general sense means ‘well-being,’ it is used in the philosophy of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) in a technical sense.
A person desirous of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् has to know three things: tattva or Reality, हित or the means of attaining the Reality and puruṣārtha or the nature of final attainment or मुक्ति.
One who is interested in हित should be aware of five things such as svasvarūpa (one’s own nature), parasvarūpa (nature of God) and so on.
See VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA for details.
